title: Belgrade, 1961: Non-Alignment Begins

endcard.line: Pictures: Kosta Miličević (public domain); Foreign Ministry of the Republic of Indonesia (public domain)

segments.say: In September nineteen sixty-one, twenty-five countries met in Belgrade, then in Yugoslavia. They wanted to stay out of the Cold War's two camps.

items.text: the Bandung principles still guide the movement

segments.say: The idea took shape six years earlier, at the Asian-African Conference in Bandung, Indonesia, in nineteen fifty-five.
At Bandung, newly independent nations talked about peace, economic development and the end of colonial rule, rather than taking sides between East and West.

anim.title: At the first summit
items: From Asia, Africa, Europe and Latin America
Including India, Egypt, Indonesia, Ghana and Yugoslavia

segments.say: Twenty-five countries attended the first summit, from the first to the sixth of September. India was one of them, alongside Egypt, Indonesia, Ghana and the host, Yugoslavia.
Non-alignment meant joining neither bloc, so these countries could focus on national independence and their own development.
For GS Two, remember Bandung, nineteen fifty-five, as the seed, Belgrade, nineteen sixty-one, as the founding, and India among the first members.

sources: Non-Aligned Movement, History page on the official site of Uganda's NAM Chairmanship (nam.go.ug/history): the Bandung (Asian-African) Conference was convened to discuss peace, the role of developing countries in the Cold War, economic development and decolonisation, out of a desire not to be involved in the East-West confrontation; NAM formally established at the First Summit, 1–6 September 1961, Belgrade, Yugoslavia, drawing on the Bandung principles; the 25 countries that attended (list includes Cuba, Cyprus, Egypt, Ghana, India, Indonesia, Yugoslavia); NAM's work still guided by the Bandung principles

reviewNote: Facts are from the NAM history page on Uganda's official chairmanship site (Uganda chairs NAM 2024–2027). The MEA's NAM document wasn't read here. No leaders are named, and no faces are shown, as the list asks. The 1961 summit photos on Commons all show delegates, so the video uses a painting of Belgrade (by a painter who died in 1920) and the Bandung building at night. Check the 'Latin America' card: Cuba is the only Latin American country on the 1961 list. Moving facts: NAM's chair and membership.
